title: ASP.NET Core Convention-Based Routing
description: Configure and use convention-based routing to map URLs to controllers and actions for clean, maintainable web apps.

data.text: What Is Routing?

Routing is the system that maps an incoming URL to a controller action. When a user visits `https://yourapp.com/Products/Details/5`, the routing engine looks at the URL segments, finds the matching controller (`ProductsController`) and action method (`Details`), and calls it with `id = 5`.

terms.definition: A pattern that defines how a URL maps to a controller and action.
A unit that handles a request, typically a controller action.
A part of a URL separated by slashes, e.g., Products, Details, 5.
A wildcard route segment (*catchall) that captures any remaining URL parts.
A rule that restricts what values a route segment can match, e.g., only integers.

data.caption: How ASP.NET Core routing maps a URL to a controller action.
data.definition:
flowchart LR
    A[Incoming URL] --> B{Routing Middleware}
    B -->|Match| C[Route Pattern]
    C -->|Extract| D[Controller, Action, Parameters]
    D --> E[Controller.Action Called]
    E --> F[Response Returned]
    B -->|No Match| G[404 Not Found]
    G --> A

data.text: ASP.NET Core supports two main types of routing:

items: **Convention-based routing** — routes are defined centrally in `Program.cs`. Best for traditional MVC apps.
**Attribute routing** — routes are defined directly on controllers and actions using C# attributes. Best for APIs and fine-grained control.

data.title: This Lesson Covers
data.text: Convention-based routing, route patterns, default values, optional parameters, static routes, and the catchall wildcard. Attribute routing is covered in the next lesson.
The Default Route
Every new ASP.NET Core MVC project comes with a default route already configured in `Program.cs`:

data.title: Default route in Program.cs
data.content: The default route configuration for a new ASP.NET Core MVC app.

data.text: This route pattern has three segments:

items: **action** — maps to the action method name (default: `Index`).
**id** — an optional parameter (the `?` makes it optional).

data.text: Because of the default values, visiting just `/` automatically calls `HomeController.Index()`. Visiting `/Products` calls `ProductsController.Index()`. Visiting `/Products/Details/5` calls `ProductsController.Details(5)`.
URL Segments and How They Match
A URL segment is each part of the path between slashes. For example, `/Products/Details/5` has three segments: `Products`, `Details`, and `5`. The default route matches up to three segments:

data.title: Pro Tip
data.text: If you remove the default values from the route (so it reads `{controller}/{action}/{id?}`), URLs with fewer than 2 segments will return 404. Always keep defaults if you want the home page to work.
Static Routes
You can add literal text to a route pattern to create fixed URL prefixes. This is useful for organizing sections of your site or preserving old URLs after a refactor:

data.title: Static route prefix
data.content: All URLs starting with /News go through the News prefix.

data.text: With this route, `/News` maps to `HomeController.Index()`, and `/News/Products/List` maps to `ProductsController.List()`. The `News` part is fixed and cannot be changed by the user.
Preserving Old Routes
If you rename or remove a controller, you can map old URLs to a new controller using the `defaults` parameter:

data.title: Mapping old URLs to a new controller
data.content: Redirect old /Shopping URLs to the Home controller.
data.code:
app.MapControllerRoute(
    name: "shop",
    pattern: "Shopping/{action}",
    defaults: new { controller = "Home" });

data.text: Now `/Shopping/Clothes` maps to `HomeController.Clothes()`. This is a great way to avoid breaking bookmarked links or search engine results after restructuring your controllers.
Default Values and Route Ordering
You can hard-code a controller and action by providing both default values:

data.title: Fixed URL mapping to a specific action
data.code:
app.MapControllerRoute(
    name: "legacy",
    pattern: "Old",
    defaults: new { controller = "Home", action = "Index" });

data.text: Routes are evaluated **in order**. The routing engine tries the first route, then the second, and so on. Always place the most specific routes first:

data.title: Route order matters
data.content: Put the most specific route before the general one.
data.code:
app.MapControllerRoute(
    name: "specific",
    pattern: "Shopping/Old",
    defaults: new { controller = "Home", action = "Index" });

app.MapControllerRoute(
    name: "general",
    pattern: "Shopping/{action}",
    defaults: new { controller = "Home" });

data.title: Common Mistake
data.text: If you place the general `Shopping/{action}` route first, it will match `/Shopping/Old` and call `HomeController.Old()` instead of the intended `Index()` action.
Custom Segment Variables
You can add your own segments beyond `controller`, `action`, and `id`. For example, a blog route might include a `slug` segment:

data.title: Custom route segment
data.content: Add a custom slug segment to capture blog post identifiers.

data.text: In the action method, access the custom segment value through `RouteData.Values` or by adding a matching parameter:

data.title: Reading a custom segment parameter
data.content: Access the slug parameter directly in the action method.

data.text: Optional Route Parameters
Add a `?` after a segment to make it optional. The route will still match even when that segment is missing from the URL:

data.title: Optional parameter route
data.content: The id segment is optional — both /Home/Check and /Home/Check/42 will match.

data.text: When the optional segment is missing, the action parameter will be `null` (for reference types) or the default value (for value types like `int`).
The Catchall Wildcard
The `*catchall` segment captures any remaining URL parts beyond the defined segments. It is useful for wiki-style URLs, documentation paths, or catch-all error pages:

data.title: Catchall route
data.content: Capture all remaining segments into the catchall parameter.

data.text: With this route, `/Docs/Index` sets `catchall` to `null`, while `/Docs/Index/Getting-Started/Installation` sets `catchall` to `Getting-Started/Installation`.

cards.title: Convention-Based Routing
cards.description: Routes are defined in one place (Program.cs) and apply to all controllers.
pros: Easy to change URLs in one place
cons: Can become hard to manage in large apps

cards.title: Attribute Routing
cards.description: Routes are defined directly on controllers and actions using C# attributes.
pros: Keeps the route definition next to the code
cons: Harder to see all URLs at a glance

data.title: Practice: Design a Blog Route
data.description: Create a convention-based route for a simple blog. The URL pattern should be /Blog/{year}/{month}/{slug}, and it should map to a BlogController.Post action. Also add a static route for /About that maps to HomeController.About.
steps: Add the custom route pattern in Program.cs.
Create a BlogController with a Post(string year, string month, string slug) action.
Verify that /Blog/2024/09/aspnet-core-routing calls BlogController.Post with the correct values.
data.expectedOutcome: You will understand how to build custom route patterns with multiple segments and static route prefixes.

items.text: Routes are defined in Program.cs using MapControllerRoute.
items.hint: Routes must be registered before app.Run().

items.text: Place the most specific routes first.
items.hint: Routing stops at the first match.

items.text: Use default values to make segments optional.
Use *catchall to capture long URL paths.
items.hint: Only one catchall per route, and it must be the last segment.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Convention-based routing maps URL segments to controller, action, and parameters.
Default values make segments optional; the ? suffix also makes a segment optional.
Static route prefixes help preserve old URLs or organize site sections.
Routes are matched in order — always put the most specific route first.
The *catchall wildcard captures all remaining URL segments as a single string.
data.takeaway: Convention-based routing is the foundation of every ASP.NET Core MVC app. Master it, and URLs will feel predictable and organized.
